extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, logicians, and mathematicians interested in foundations and structuralism
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly analysis of Bourbaki's conception of mathematical structuralism, its metamathematical core (species of structure, transportable relations, echelon constructions), and how frameworks such as Makkai's FOLDS can capture and extend it to categories and other modern structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuralist motto (invariance under isomorphism)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a logical theory to be considered a structuralist theory for abstract mathematics, the only properties P that are legitimate in the theory are those that satisfy invariance under isomorphism: If P(X) and X ≅ Y, then P(Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a metamathematical requirement: the invariance must be provable in the theory. Bourbaki incorporates this into the axiomatic method by requiring that defining relations of a structure be invariant under transport (isomorphism). It is offered as the core criterion that separates structuralist theories from non-structuralist ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species of structure must be given by a text plus a transportable relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A Bourbaki 'species of structure' in the language of set theory is a text (a series of first-order formulas in a given signature L) together with a transportable relation R, the latter being the axiom of the species of structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, one supplies a signature (principal/auxiliary base sets, specified sorts, relation symbols) and an axiom (text) whose relation is transportable. One must verify (provably in the theory) that the relation is transportable (i.e., invariant under the appropriate notion of transport/isomorphism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportable relation (transport of relation / isomorphism-invariance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A transportable relation is one whose definition does not depend on any specific property of the underlying sets but only on how elements enter the relation; equivalently, the relation is preserved under canonical bijections/transport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourbaki requires that the relations used in the axioms of a structure provably be transportable. The verification that a relation is transportable can be a nontrivial metamathematical exercise (e.g., showing that ordinary definitions like homeomorphism follow from the general notion of transport).

rubrics_metrics.name: Echelon construction and signature formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: To define a type of structure Bourbaki starts with a finite list of set variables/constants and forms an echelon construction (closure under products and power sets), picks specified sorts from it, and adds sorted relation symbols to yield a signature L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This syntactic setup (echelon, sorts, relations) provides the basic terms needed to express the axioms of many abstract structures; it is the technical device for covering diverse structure types (algebraic, topological, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamathematical stance: definitions and verification must be at the metamathematical level
rubrics_metrics.description: Bourbaki's proper analysis of structure is metamathematical: the notion of species of structure, transportability, and invariance are properties of the defining text/formulas and must be demonstrated in the metatheory rather than merely asserted informally on the object level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of conflating the mathematical (object-level) presentation of a structure with Bourbaki's metamathematical requirements. Many commentators read Bourbaki as if everything were just set-theoretic at the object level; Bourbaki's point is that the transport/invariance conditions are metatheoretic constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic method as generator of structural insight
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiomatic method's essential aim is to abstract common ideas across theories, to reveal 'forms' (structures) that reorganize mathematics and provide intelligibility beyond mere formal logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use axiomatic abstraction to identify 'mother structures' and to group partial theories; the axiomatic method is not merely deductive formalism but a creative method that yields organization, economy of thought, and transfer of general theorems to particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of mother structures and hierarchical organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics should be organized by 'mother structures' (Bourbaki suggested families like composition, continuity, comparison) with a hierarchy from simple/general to complex/particular, and specialized structures obtained by adding axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion guides what to look for when structuring mathematical theories: recognize base (mother) structures, their families, how additional axioms produce descendants (e.g., abelian groups from groups), and how multiple structures combine organically rather than by juxtaposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structures as tools: verify applicability to problems (economy of thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structures are tools: once one recognizes that a given mathematical situation fits a known structure type, one may immediately apply the entire arsenal of general theorems belonging to that structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate structural analyses by their epistemic virtues—organization, better understanding, efficiency, and transferability—i.e., whether they reduce ad hoc computations and make results reusable across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodation of categories and equivalence (generalize transport notion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because category-theoretic identity is often given by equivalence rather than strict isomorphism, a satisfactory structuralist framework must generalize Bourbaki's transport notion so it handles categories (and higher structures) appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourbaki's original transport notion is inadequate for categories; a metamathematical framework must be able to produce the correct criterion of identity (equivalence of categories, biequivalence, homotopy equivalence) for the structures under study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal framework should derive identity from signature (FOLDS proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Makkai's FOLDS (First-Order Logic with Dependent Sorts) is proposed as a revision of first-order logic: multi-sorted with dependent sorts, where identity/isomorphism is not given a priori but derived from the signature and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using FOLDS one can obtain appropriate notions of identity for sets, categories, bicategories, homotopy theory, etc., and thereby prove an invariance principle: if M satisfies φ and M is L-isomorphic to N then N satisfies φ. FOLDS is offered as a formal, metamathematical solution that captures Bourbaki's core requirements and extends them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-endedness and evolvability of fundamental structures
rubrics_metrics.description: A structuralist conception should be open-ended: future developments may increase the number of fundamental structures and reveal new fruitful axioms or combinations of axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of structuralism should allow that the list of 'fundamental' structures is not fixed; the framework should accommodate emergence of novel structures and novel interplays (e.g., interactions made explicit by category theory).
